text:
Thanks. I found Q3 fairly clear overall, though thinking about *how* Absalon data would be used felt a bit vague – what specifically are we tracking? It’s easy to slip into surveillance territory there.

For me, the explainability questions (Q4) are most critical. As an international student navigating a new system and working part-time, I need to understand *why* any intervention is suggested; trust is key. 

I was surprised everyone was so willing to accept some loss of accuracy for fairness (Q5). While important, a large drop feels counterproductive. Perhaps offering students agency – an opt-out mechanism – could address those concerns and retain more overall effectiveness? I also answered ‘small’ on nationality while many said ‘never’, reflecting my belief that understanding diverse backgrounds *can* help tailor support without being intrusive.

Thanks. I agree with S2 about Q3 – the Absalon data felt a little too broad; specifying *what* activity we’re looking at would be helpful. As an advisor, I see the potential for misinterpreting that data easily.

For me, Q3.5 and Q3.6 – the sensitive data questions - are most important. The strong consensus against using age, gender or race is reassuring, but the moderate acceptance of first-gen status/financial aid with caveats feels right; those *can* indicate barriers to success *if* handled carefully and ethically.

I was a bit surprised by the willingness to accept even a 5% drop in accuracy for fairness (Q5.1). While I agree fairness is paramount, it highlights how crucial good data quality and rigorous bias testing are *before* we ever deploy this model - perhaps investing in those areas could minimise that loss.

Thanks to both S2 and A1. I agree with the points about needing more specificity around the Absalon data – it feels like a slippery slope otherwise. As someone managing a chronic health condition *while* studying, I found Q3.5 particularly difficult. While my disability impacts my studies, I'm very hesitant about having that information used in any predictive model, even with assurances of privacy. The 'small improvement' threshold felt… insufficient to justify it.

I think Q4, explainability, is key. My experience navigating the university’s support systems shows me how important clear communication is. And yes, I was also surprised by the relatively high acceptance of accuracy loss for fairness – I feel strongly about avoiding perpetuating disadvantage *but* we need to maximize help available overall too. Perhaps a tiered system of interventions, based on confidence level, would be useful?

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite clear, although like others said, specifying *what* Absalon data is used is vital – it’s easy to feel monitored. For me, though, Q3.5 was hardest. As someone with a long-term mental health condition affecting my studies, I answered ‘small’ for disability, but reluctantly. It feels risky; being flagged could be stigmatizing. 

I think explainability (Q4) is most crucial. Understanding *why* the model flags me helps me trust any support offered. I also agree with S3 about a tiered intervention system – higher confidence levels warrant more proactive outreach. The group’s willingness to accept accuracy loss for fairness (Q5) is admirable, but reflects my own anxiety about being overlooked if the bar’s too high.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 generally clear, though like others, specifying *what* Absalon data would be tracked feels vital - we need to avoid creeping surveillance. For me, the questions around sensitive data (Q3.5 & Q3.6) are paramount. As an advisor for eleven years, I've seen how systemic inequalities impact students. While a small improvement isn’t enough justification for using disability data, first-gen/financial aid status *can* be legitimate indicators, but require careful ethical oversight.

I largely agree with the group on explainability (Q4) being crucial; building trust is essential for effective advising. And the discussion around accuracy vs. fairness (Q5) highlights a real tension – minimizing harm *and* maximizing help are both priorities. An opt-out mechanism, as S2 suggested, could be vital to address this.

Thanks everyone. I agree with A2 about the need for ethical oversight around financial aid and first-generation status – those are factors I see impacting students *constantly* in my advising role. Q3 felt generally clear, though I share the concern about specifying what Absalon data would be used; it’s too easy to imagine that becoming invasive.

For me, Q4 - explainability - is most important. As an advisor, I need to be able to *explain* why a student has been flagged to them, and address their concerns. The near-universal preference for at least *some* explanation is reassuring. 

I answered ‘small’ on first-gen/financial aid data because it can provide valuable context. My slight disagreement with the “never” responses on nationality – while I respect those privacy concerns – stems from seeing how cultural adjustment impacts student success; understanding that *could* inform support, carefully.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 fairly clear, although the Absalon data point does feel a bit broad – knowing *what* activity they’d be tracking would be important. The questions about sensitive data (Q3.5) were definitely the hardest. Having dropped out of university once already, and being an international student learning Danish, I’m very aware of feeling ‘different’. I answered 'small' for first-gen status & financial aid – those experiences *do* create barriers. But I said “never” for everything else; my background makes me cautious about sharing personal details.

Explainability (Q4) is vital. Coming to a new system, understanding why I’m flagged helps build trust. And I agree with the opt-out idea—giving students agency seems crucial.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 quite clear overall, though like others, specifying *what* Absalon data would be used feels important – it's easy to feel watched when you’re still adjusting to a new university system. As an international student, I definitely prioritized privacy in the sensitive data questions (Q3.5). While first-generation status or financial aid might offer some context, even with small improvements, I leaned towards ‘never’ for things like nationality and especially age or disability; it feels too intrusive.

For me, explainability (Q4) is *most* important. Coming from a different educational system, understanding why the model identifies difficulties helps build trust in any support offered. The group's willingness to accept accuracy loss for fairness resonates – being overlooked is a real concern, but privacy must come first.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 mostly clear, though agreeing with the point about needing specifics on Absalon data – it feels a bit ‘big brother’ otherwise. Honestly, Q3.5 was *really* hard. Having ADHD and having dropped out once before, I'm acutely aware of how easily things can derail. I answered 'small' for disability because I think understanding challenges *can* help, but only if it doesn't lead to stigma or assumptions. 

Explainability (Q4) is huge for me too. A lack of transparency feels invalidating. And the accuracy/fairness trade-off (Q5)? Definitely leaning towards fairness, even with a small loss in overall identification. I’d much rather fewer students be wrongly flagged than perpetuate existing inequalities, especially knowing how anxiety-inducing these systems can be.

Thanks everyone. I found Q3 pretty clear overall, though like others, specifying *what* Absalon data would be tracked feels important – it's easy to feel monitored when you’re still getting used to things. Having dropped out once and restarted my master’s, the questions about sensitive data (Q3.5) were tough. I answered ‘small’ for nationality and first-gen status because those experiences *can* create real challenges, but everything else was a “never”.

I think explainability (Q4) is absolutely key. Knowing *why* I’m flagged would be crucial to trust any support offered, especially given my past experience with dropping out. And I strongly agree with the idea of an opt-out mechanism - giving students control feels essential.

Thanks everyone, that was really insightful. I found Q3 fairly clear overall, though the Absalon data point definitely needs more detail - it feels a little too broad right now. For me, Q3.5 was the hardest; as someone with dyslexia and receiving extra time on exams, I’m very aware of being labelled ‘different’. I reluctantly answered ‘small’ for disability, but it felt risky. 

I think explainability (Q4) is *critical*. Understanding why I'm flagged, especially given my learning difference, would build trust. I agree with the group about fairness (Q5), and the opt-out idea sounds excellent. The overall willingness to prioritize fairness over sheer accuracy feels reassuring.

Thanks everyone, that was a really helpful discussion. I found Q3 mostly clear, although the specifics of what Absalon data would be used definitely need more thought – it's easy to see how that could become intrusive. As someone who dropped out and is restarting my studies, I was most concerned with the sensitive data questions (Q3.5). I answered ‘small’ for first-gen/financial aid because those *can* create barriers, but I strongly feel age, gender, nationality & disability should never be used – it's too risky.

Explainability (Q4) is vital; understanding *why* I’m flagged helps me trust the support offered. And I wholeheartedly agree with the opt-out suggestion; students deserve agency over their data and interventions.
